concepts.title: latent variables
concepts.one_liner: The vector $\mathbf{z}$ is a vector of latent variables, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label.
concepts.content: Usually we draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a simple distribution such as Gaussian noise, that is, $p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1})$. The way to think of $\mathbf{z}$ is that it is a vector of **latent variables**, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images $\mathbf{x}$ and their labels $\mathbf{y}$). In our example, $\mathbf{y}$ tells $g$ to make a bird but the $\mathbf{z}$-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ capture unobserved image attributes, enabling generators to produce diverse outputs beyond given labels.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models use a corruption process that adds noise step-by-step to data and train a neural net to reverse this process, turning noise back into data.
concepts.content:
The strategy of autoregressive models is to break a hard problem into lots of simple pieces. Diffusion models are another class of model that uses this same strategy. They can be understood by looking at autoregressive models in reverse: starting with a complete image, autoregressive models remove one pixel at a time, which is a signal corruption process. Diffusion models use a different corruption process: starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to produce a noisy image $\mathbf{x}_1$, then add more noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to get $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise is isotropic Gaussian noise. After $T$ steps, the image $\mathbf{x}_T$ looks like pure noise if $T$ is large enough. Specifically, if the noise process is $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_t &= \sqrt{(1-\beta_t)}\mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\mathbf{\epsilon}_t\\
    \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})
\end{aligned}$$ with $\beta_t \leq 1$, then $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ as $T \rightarrow \infty$. Diffusion models train a neural net $f_{\theta}$ to reverse this process by supervised learning on sequences of images becoming noisier. For example, the sequence of images of a bird getting noisier can be reversed to provide training pairs mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$, which $f_{\theta}$ learns to predict. This neural net is called a denoiser; it learns to remove noise from an image. Applying the denoiser repeatedly starting from pure noise should produce a noise-less image resembling training data. The training steps are: 1. Generate training data by corrupting images (forward noising). 2. Train a neural net to invert each corruption step (reverse denoising). It helps to let the denoiser observe the time step $t$ as input, so we have $$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$$ which improves predictions by informing the model how noisy the input is. The denoiser can be trained using an $L_2$ loss or to output Gaussian parameters, yielding probabilistic interpretations. A useful trick is to reparameterize the learning problem to predict the noise rather than the signal: $$\begin{aligned}
    f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t \\
    \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t
\end{aligned}$$ Diffusion models learn a mapping from pure noise to data by creating training sequences from data to noise, which is easier to do than generating data from noise directly.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models exist to generate complex data (like images) by learning to reverse a noise corruption process, which is easier than directly generating structured data from noise. This approach provides a principled way to train models that create realistic samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Diffusion models corrupt data by adding noise step-by-step until it becomes pure noise.
- A neural net denoiser is trained to reverse this process, removing noise gradually.
- Training involves supervised learning on pairs of noisy and less noisy images, enabling generation from noise to data.

Then they repeat this process, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise is isotropic Gaussian noise.

It is very hard to figure out how to create structured data out of noise, but it is easy to do the reverse, turning data into noise.

concepts.title: GAN learning problem
concepts.one_liner: The GAN learning problem is formulated as a minimax game between the generator and discriminator.
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating GAN training as a minimax game captures the adversarial nature where the generator tries to fool the discriminator and the discriminator tries to detect fakes.
concepts.recap_md:
- GAN training is a minimax optimization problem.
- The discriminator maximizes classification accuracy.
- The generator minimizes the discriminator's ability to detect fakes.

concepts.title: GANs are Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs learn mappings from latent noise to samples, amortizing optimization unlike hand-defined statistical image models.
concepts.content: GANs are related to the image and texture models we saw in earlier sections. For example, the Heeger-Bergen model synthesizes images with the same statistics as a source texture by optimizing image pixels until certain statistics match those of a training image. In the Heeger-Bergen model, the objective is to match subband histograms. In the language of GANs, the loss that checks for such a match is a kind of discriminator; it outputs a score related to the difference between a generated image's statistics and the real image's statistics. However, unlike a GAN, this discriminator is hand-defined in terms of certain statistics rather than learned. Additionally, GANs amortize the optimization via learning: GANs learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples rather than arriving at samples via an optimization process starting from scratch each time we want a new sample.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs provide a learned approach to synthesizing images with desired statistics, improving upon hand-crafted statistical models by learning a direct mapping from noise to samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- GANs relate to statistical image models like Heeger-Bergen.
- Heeger-Bergen matches image statistics via optimization with a hand-defined discriminator.
- GANs learn a mapping from noise to samples, amortizing optimization.

concepts.title: Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data.
concepts.content:
Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data. This density function may play a role in training the generator (e.g., we want the generator to produce samples from $p_{\theta}$), or the density function may be the goal itself (e.g., we want to be able to estimate the probability of datapoints in order to detect anomalies).

In fact, some generative models *only* produce a density $p_{\theta}$ and do not learn any explicit generator function. Instead, samples can be drawn from $p_{\theta}$ using a sampling algorithm, such as **Markov Chain Monte Carlo** (**MCMC**), that takes a density as input and produce samples from it as output. concepts.title: divergence
concepts.one_liner: A divergence $D$ measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples from $p_{\texttt{data}}$.
concepts.content:

$$\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} D(p_{\theta}, p_{\texttt{data}})$$
The problem is that we do not actually have the function $p_{\texttt{data}}$, we only have samples from this function, $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$. Therefore, we need a divergence $D$ that measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples from $p_{\texttt{data}}$. 

The divergence need not be a proper distance *metric*, and often is not; it can be nonsymmetric, where $D(p,q) \neq D(q,p)$, and need not satisfy the triangle-inequality. In fact, a divergence is defined by just two properties: nonnegativity and $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.motivation_md: Divergences allow comparing model distributions to data distributions using only samples, enabling optimization without explicit knowledge of the data distribution function.

concepts.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence
concepts.one_liner: A common choice is to use the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which is defined as follows:
concepts.content:
A common choice is to use the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**, which is defined as follows: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\Big[-\log \frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})}\Big]\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})\big]\\
    &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] \quad \triangleleft \quad\text{dropped second term since no dependence on $p_{\theta}$}
    \\
    &\approx \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$${#eq-generative_models-max_likelihood} where the final line is an empirical estimate of the
expectation by sampling over the training dataset
concepts.motivation_md: KL divergence is widely used to measure how one distribution approximates another, enabling maximum likelihood estimation from data samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- KL divergence measures difference between $p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $p_{\theta}$.  
- Minimizing KL divergence corresponds to maximizing expected log-likelihood.  
- Empirical estimate uses sample average over training data.

concepts.title: Energy-Based Models
concepts.one_liner: Energy-based models learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$ and use it to define relative probabilities without computing the normalizing constant.
concepts.content:
Density models constrain the learned function to be normalized, that is, $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. This constraint is often hard to realize. One approach is to learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$, then convert it to the normalized density $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, where $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$ is the normalizing constant. The $Z(\theta)$ can be very expensive to compute and often can only be approximated.

The parametric form $\frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$ is sometimes referred to as a **Boltzmann** or **Gibbs distribution**.

Notice that $Z$ is a function of model parameters $\theta$ but not of datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, since we integrate over all possible data values.

Note that low energy $\Rightarrow$ high probability. So we minimize energy to maximize probability.

**Energy-based models** (**EBM**s) address this by simply skipping the step where we normalize the density, and letting the output of the learner just be $E_\theta$. Even though it is not a true probability density, $E_{\theta}$ can still be used for many of the applications we would want a density for. This is because we can compare *relative probabilities* with $E_\theta$: 

$$\begin{aligned}    \frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)} = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}/Z(\theta)}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}/Z(\theta)}
    = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}}
\end{aligned}$$ Knowing relative probabilities is all that is required for sampling (via MCMC), for outlier detection (the relatively lowest probability datapoint in a set of datapoints is the outlier), and even for optimizing over a space of of data to find the datapoint that is max probability (because $\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}} -E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$).

concepts.title: contrastive divergence
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive divergence modifies the energy function to decrease energy on data samples and increase energy on model samples, approximating the gradient of the log likelihood function.
concepts.content:
One way to fit an energy function to observed data is called contrastive divergence. On each iteration of optimization, this method modifies the energy function to decrease the energy assigned to samples from the data (positive term) and to increase the energy assigned to samples from the model (i.e., samples from the energy function itself; negative term), as shown in @fig-generative_models-contrastive_divergence:

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood energy function to data, using contrastive divergence. @hinton2002training)

Once the energy function perfectly adheres to the data, samples from the model are identical to samples from the data and the positive and negative terms cancel out. This makes intuitive sense because we don't want the energy function to change once we have perfectly fit the data. Mathematically, this procedure is an approximation to the gradient of the log likelihood function.

Defining $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, start by decomposing the gradient of the log likelihood into two terms, which will play the role of positive and negative terms:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(\theta)}]\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] - \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta)
\end{aligned}$$

The first term is the positive term gradient, which tries to modify parameters to decrease the energy placed on data samples. The second term is the negative term gradient; it appears as an intractable integral, so we rewrite it as an expectation, which can be approximated via sampling:

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\nabla_{\theta}Z(\theta) \\
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} \int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $Z$}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \int_x \nabla_{\theta} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{exchange sum and grad}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} -\int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $p_{\theta}$}\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of expectation}
\end{aligned}$$

In @eq-generative_models-grad_log_identity we use a useful identity from the chain rule of calculus: $\nabla_{x} \log f(x) = \frac{1}{f(x)} \nabla_{x} f(x)$.

Plugging @eq-generative_models-cd_neg back into @eq-generative_models-cd, we get:

$$\begin{aligned}  \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]
\end{aligned}$$

Both expectations can be approximated via sampling: defining $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, and taking $N$ such samples, we have

$$\begin{aligned}
    -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &\approx -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)})\\
    &= \frac{1}{N} \nabla_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}))
\end{aligned}$$

This shows the intuition: we contrast data samples and current model samples, then update the model to decrease this contrast, bringing the model closer to the data. Once $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}$ are identically distributed, this gradient will be zero in expectation; we have perfectly fit the data and no further updates should be taken.

Under our formalization of a learning problem as an objective, hypothesis space, and optimizer, contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for max likelihood objectives over energy functions. It tells us how to approximate the gradient of the likelihood function, which can then be plugged into any gradient descent method.

\nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} \int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $Z$}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \int_x \nabla_{\theta} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{exchange sum and grad}\\
    &= \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} -\int_x e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}}{Z(\theta)} \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}\\
    &= -\int_x p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of $p_{\theta}$}\\
    &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{definition of expectation}
\end{aligned}$$

In @eq-generative_models-grad_log_identity we use a useful identity from the chain rule of calculus: $\nabla_{x} \log f(x) = \frac{1}{f(x)} \nabla_{x} f(x)$.

Plugging @eq-generative_models-cd_neg back into @eq-generative_models-cd, we get:

$$\begin{aligned}  \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]
\end{aligned}$$

Both expectations can be approximated via sampling: defining $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, and taking $N$ such samples, we have

$$\begin{aligned}
    -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &\approx -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)})\\
    &= \frac{1}{N} \nabla_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}))
\end{aligned}$$

This shows the intuition: we contrast data samples and current model samples, then update the model to decrease this contrast, bringing the model closer to the data. Once $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}$ are identically distributed, this gradient will be zero in expectation; we have perfectly fit the data and no further updates should be taken.

Under our formalization of a learning problem as an objective, hypothesis space, and optimizer, contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for max likelihood objectives over energy functions. It tells us how to approximate the gradient of the likelihood function, which can then be plugged into any gradient descent method.

concepts.title: Gaussian Density Models
concepts.one_liner: One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is: $p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}$.
concepts.content:
One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}
\end{aligned}$$

This density has two parameters $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, which are the mean and variance of the distribution. The normalization constant $Z$ ensures that the function is normalized. This is the typical strategy in defining density models: create a parameterized family of functions such that any function in the family is normalized. Given such a family, we search over the parameters to optimize a generative modeling objective.

For density models, the most common objective is max likelihood:

$$\begin{aligned}
     \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(x)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

For a 1D Gaussian, this has a simple form:

$$\begin{aligned}
     \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} = -\log(Z) + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)
\end{aligned}$$

Optimizing with respect to $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ could be done via gradient descent or random search, but in this case there is also an analytical solution we can find by setting the gradient to zero. For $\theta_1^*$ we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_1^*} = 0\\
    \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)/(2\theta_2^*) = 0\\
    \sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)} - \sum_{i=1}^N \theta_1^* = 0\\
    \theta_1^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)}
\end{aligned}$$

For $\theta_2^*$ we note that $Z$ depends on $\theta_2^*$ and in particular that $\frac{\partial (-\log Z)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*}$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = 0\\
    \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*} - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)^2 = 0\\
    2\theta_2^* - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2 = 0\\
    \theta_2^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2
\end{aligned}$$

You might recognize the solutions for $\theta_1^*$ and $\theta_2^*$ as the empirical mean and variance of the data, respectively. This makes sense: to maximize the probability of the data under a Gaussian, we should set the mean and variance of the Gaussian to be the empirical mean and variance of the data.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models synthesize images pixel by pixel, predicting each pixel based on previously generated pixels.
concepts.content:
A single Gaussian is a very limited model, and the real utility of Gaussians only shows up when they are part of a larger modeling framework. Next we consider a recipe for building highly expressive models out of simple ones called an autoregressive model.

The idea of an autoregressive model is to synthesize an image pixel by pixel. Each new pixel is decided based on the sequence already generated. This is a sequence prediction problem: given a sequence of observed pixels, predict the color of the next one. We use the same learned function $f_{\theta}$ to make each subsequent prediction.

@fig-generative_models-autoregressive_prediction_schematic shows this setup. We predict each next pixel from the partial image already completed. The red bordered region is the context the prediction is based on. This context could be the entire image synthesized so far or a smaller region, like shown here. The green bordered pixel is the one we are predicting given this context. In this example, we always predict the bottom-center pixel in the context window. After making our prediction, we decide what color pixel to add to the image based on that prediction; we may add the color predicted as most likely, or sample from the predicted distribution to get randomness. Then, to predict the next missing pixel we slide the context over by one and repeat.

(see figure: An autoregressive model, $f_{\theta}$, that generates an image pixel by pixel. The black pixels are the remaining pixels to synthesize. Compare with the Efros-Leung model in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.)

This setup resembles the Efros-Leung texture synthesis algorithm, which was also an autoregressive model. The Efros-Leung algorithm was a nonparametric method that worked by stealing pixels from matching regions of an exemplar texture. Now we see how to do autoregressive modeling with a learned, parametric prediction function $f_{\theta}$, such as a deep net.

These models can be understood by first considering synthesizing one pixel, then two, and so on. It's easy to synthesize a single grayscale pixel, which can take on 256 possible values (for 8-bit grayscale). A categorical distribution can represent the probability that the pixel takes each possible value. Fitting this categorical distribution to training data amounts to counting how often each value occurs and normalizing.

To model the distribution over a second grayscale pixel given the first, we model $p(\mathbf{x_2} \mid \mathbf{x_1})$ where $\mathbf{x_1}$ is the first pixel and $\mathbf{x_2}$ is the second. Treating $\mathbf{x}_2$ as a categorical variable, we use softmax regression, as seen in @sec-intro_to_learning-image_classification.

For the third pixel conditioned on the first two, we again model a 256-way softmax regression conditioned on observations. Inductively, modeling each next pixel in the sequence is a softmax regression problem modeling
$p(\mathbf{x}_n \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})$. The cross-entropy loss is computed as in @fig-generative_models-autoregressive_softmax_regression.

(see figure: Autoregressive prediction as next-pixel-classification.)

For color images, we predict three values per pixel (red, green, blue) sequentially: first predict red as a 256-way classification, sample it, then predict green, and so on. To turn an image into a pixel sequence, a common method is vectorizing the 2D grid row by row.

We can model the probability of each subsequent pixel given preceding pixels. To generate an image, sample the first pixel, then the second given the first, then the third given the first two, etc. This is a valid model of the joint distribution $p(\mathbf{X})$ according to the chain rule of probability, which factorizes any joint distribution into a product of conditionals:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \mid \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})
\end{aligned}$$

As a convenience, define $p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) = p(\mathbf{x}_1)$ when $i=1$. This factorization shows that sequential sampling draws a valid sample from $p(\mathbf{X})$ because all conditional distributions are independent of each other.

concepts.title: chain rule of probability
concepts.one_liner: The chain rule of probability factorizes any joint distribution into a product of conditional distributions.
concepts.content:
Sampling a valid sample from $p(\mathbf{X})$ can be done according to the chain rule of probability. This rule allows us to factorize any joint distribution into a product of conditionals as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \mid \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\
    p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1})
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Sampling from Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from autoregressive models is done sequentially by sampling each pixel conditioned on previously sampled pixels.
concepts.content:
Autoregressive models give us an explicit density function, @eq-generative_models-autoregressive_likelihood. To sample from this density, we use the process described previously: sample the first pixel from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then conditioned on this pixel, sample the second from $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)$, and so forth. Since each of these densities is a categorical distribution, sampling is easy: one option is to partition a unit line segment into regions of length equal to the categorical probabilities and see where a uniform random draw along this line falls.

Autoregressive models do not have latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, which makes them incompatible with applications that involve extracting or manipulating latent variables.

- Sampling proceeds sequentially from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \mid \mathbf{x}_1)$, etc.
- Each conditional distribution is categorical, allowing straightforward sampling.
- Autoregressive models lack latent variables, limiting some applications.
